he_said_of_this_record.title_as_transcribed: a solo recording for Riverside … my first recording of Cole Porter
he_said_of_this_record.what_he_says: Riverside heard him playing solo piano in Berkshires hotels in 1954 and wanted a solo album. It was their first recording and his. He wanted a trio, they argued, and they compromised on piano and bass with Sam Gill. He said he was always reluctant to play solo because he grew up with the royalty of the piano.
he_said_of_this_record.pull_quote: But, they heard me in solo piano in 1954 and Riverside Records; they wanted me to do a solo album. I didn’t want to do a solo album, I wanted a trio and we argued about that. Finally, we compromised with myself and Sam Gill on bass. So, my first recording of Cole Porter was piano and bass, but they wanted me to do solo piano.

more_quotes.quote: My very first recording, Riverside records heard me in the Berkshires. I did their first recording, and my first recording.
But I’m happy that people like me doing solo piano, but I was always reluctant because, like I said, I grew up with the heavyweights.

he_said_of_this_record.discrepancies: The transcript contradicts itself: 'I did a solo recording for Riverside' (309856), but then the first Riverside record was a compromise for piano and bass with Sam Gill (309882). As far as I know Weston made no solo album for Riverside. 'their first recording' is Weston's claim and is not verified.

he_said_of_this_record.what_he_says: He called the live date with his idol Coleman Hawkins at the Five Spot 'another miracle'. Melba Liston wrote the arrangements from a hospital in California, and the music arrived on the day of the Monday-night recording. There was no time to rehearse, but the musicians played beautifully.
he_said_of_this_record.pull_quote: What happened was, the recording took place on a Monday night at the Five Spot, and there was no time for rehearsal. She was in the hospital in California, and by some miracle the music arrived the day of the recording. I passed out the music, no time to rehearse, but I had such great musicians that they played beautifully.

more_quotes.quote: A good example of that is this, when we did the date with Coleman Hawkins, which was another miracle for me because Coleman Hawkins was my idol.

he_said_of_this_record.what_he_says: He said he wanted the record to bring the ancestors, who are very much alive, to everybody. He wrote the whole concept and realised only Melba Liston could arrange it. She was in a wheelchair after a stroke and could no longer play trombone, so he goaded her into doing the arrangements 'stroke or no stroke'. With her aunt Thelma's help she learned to write music on the computer with her left hand.
he_said_of_this_record.title_meaning: The ancestors, who are very much alive; the royalty of Armstrong, Bolden and Ellington, going back to Africa.
he_said_of_this_record.pull_quote: I wanted to do this recording, “Spirit of Our Ancestors”, again, trying to bring the ancestors to everybody. They are very much alive.

more_quotes.quote: Then I realized that only Melba Liston could do this. She was in a wheelchair, she had been paralyzed on one side, and she can no longer play the trombone. I went to see her, and I insulted her as only musicians can do. I called her all kinds of names. I said to her, “You have to do these arrangements stroke or no stroke, handicap or no handicap,” you know? She cried a little bit, you know?
But, it turned out her aunt Thelma was a computer specialist and Melba started studying the computer and how to write the music with her left hand.
What Louie Armstrong and Buddy Boland, and Duke Ellington, all they created, that’s our royalty going back to Africa itself.

he_said_of_this_record.discrepancies: The published title is 'The Spirits of Our Ancestors' (Antilles, early 1990s). Weston brings it up in answer to a question set in '97', so the transcript places it later than its actual release. Names in the same block are transcribed by ear: 'Louie Armstrong' is Louis Armstrong and 'Buddy Boland' is Buddy Bolden.

he_said_of_this_record.what_he_says: He recorded Saga for Verve in Paris; the title came from the name of the African shop of the woman he later married, and he said 'saga' means family, which is what all his music is geared towards. He named Billy Higgins, Neil Clarke, Alex Blake, Billy Harper, T.K. Blue and Benny Powell, said most of the songs were his originals, and that Stereo Review chose it number one. Asked whether family tied the songs together, he said all his recordings carry the history of the music as Africa's contribution, with the blues underneath.
he_said_of_this_record.title_meaning: Named after his future wife's African shop, 'Saga'; in language the word means family.
he_said_of_this_record.pull_quote: At the time “Saga” came, actually, from the name of an African shop that my wife, who I married afterwards, her shop was called “Saga”. Saga, in the world of language means family. All of my music is geared towards family, because I think that is so important, and that’s what I learned from my ancestors.

more_quotes.quote: It was, for me, a very wonderful, wonderful date. It was chosen number one by Stereo Review Magazine.
So, all of my compositions, all of my music is based upon love, history, and family, and respect.
The blues is always underneath it all because the blues, I feel, is the language of our people, how we survived.

he_said_of_this_record.discrepancies: 'Jean Philippe Alad', called 'the president of Verve', is evidently Jean-Philippe Allard, the Verve (France) producer with whom Weston made his Verve/Gitanes albums; 'president' is Weston's word.

he_said_of_this_record.what_he_says: Asked about the 1997 Earth Birth record, he identified it as 'that one with strings'. Jenkins said it was part of a residency at the Montreal Jazz Festival that year, for which Weston said Melba Liston did all the arrangements.
he_said_of_this_record.pull_quote: So, what took place in Montreal was a smaller version of that. We got 25 strings of the Montreal Symphony Orchestra, Billy Higgins, Christian McBride, and myself.

raw: Khepera is an album by the American pianist Randy Weston , released in 1998.
Recorded in March 1998, the album was produced by Weston and Brian Bacchus.
Weston played many songs at a 6 8 time.

he_said_of_this_record.what_he_says: He said Khepera is an ancient Egyptian word meaning to regenerate: to win back the human contact lost to machines. He met the pipa player Min Xiao-Fen through her work with a Senegalese musician in Atlanta. Dr. Wayne Chandler's book Ancient Future and a Guggenheim exhibition of Shang masks convinced them both of an ancient Africa–China connection, and the record was built to make that connection. Pharoah Sanders, Chief Bey, Victor Lewis, Alex Blake and Benny Powell played, and Melba Liston arranged.
he_said_of_this_record.title_meaning: An ancient Egyptian word meaning to regenerate, to bring back the senses: a return to human contact.
he_said_of_this_record.pull_quote: “Khepera” is a way saying that we have to bring that back, to regenerate, to clean ourselves and come back, to get back to human contact.

more_quotes.quote: Well, “Khepera” is like an ancient Egyptian word that means “like to regenerate, to bring back out senses.” We become so involved with machines that we loose that human contact that we had before.
So “Khepera” consisted of connecting China and Africa, which, people just can’t believe the connection.
So, “Khepera” is a very, very spiritual word.

he_said_of_this_record.discrepancies: 'Pharaoh Sanders' is Pharoah Sanders. 'Love The History Of' is 'Love, the Mystery Of', Guy Warren's composition and Weston's theme song. 'Mortiem', the Senegalese musician in Atlanta, is probably the percussionist Mor Thiam.

he_said_of_this_record.what_he_says: He brought six Gnawa to New York, three from Tangier and three from Marrakech, for a concert in a Christian church on Lafayette Avenue in Brooklyn. Babatunde Olatunji opened with his dancers and musicians, and then Weston's group played with the Gnawa. He said Yoruba, Islam and Christianity were present together through music, before an audience of every denomination, colour, age and gender.

more_quotes.quote: It was powerful because we all experience a very powerful experience to see the whole connection of humanity, which can only happened with music.
With music you don’t have to read to music, you don’t have to see to music, you just hear and you feel.
I had these six Gnawa come to New York for concerts; three were from Tangiers, three from Marrakech.

he_said_of_this_record.what_he_says: He said the solo piano record took its idea from Dr. Wayne Chandler's book: to go ahead we have to go back and know where we came from as a human race. He set this against a world hung up on machines, cell phones and buttons, and said he plays as he does because of human contact with masters such as Monk, Basie, Hawkins and Gillespie. Asked why it was solo, he traced his solo playing to the 1974 festival, the Berkshires and Antibes, and said 'maybe with this one, I wanted to express something by doing solo piano'.
he_said_of_this_record.title_meaning: From Wayne Chandler's book: in order to go ahead we have to go back.
he_said_of_this_record.pull_quote: The whole idea from “Ancient Future” is for us to go ahead we have to know where we came from as a human race, and where we are going to go.

more_quotes.quote: That wonderful book that Dr. Wayne Chandler wrote, which says that in order for us to go ahead we have got to go back.
The purpose of “Ancient Future” was inspired by that book to somehow bring us back.
Maybe with this one, I wanted to express something by doing solo piano.

he_said_of_this_record.title_as_transcribed: a concert live in St. Lucia
he_said_of_this_record.what_he_says: Jenkins called it his most recent recording with his regular ensemble, an outdoor concert in St. Lucia also issued on DVD. Weston said the hot weather, the audience and the climate made it wonderful. They played his usual songs, which he defended as carrying eternal messages, as Duke Ellington's did.
he_said_of_this_record.pull_quote: In a warm climate, you know, like St. Lucia, it was wonderful. There was a lot of energy and everybody felt really good.

more_quotes.quote: Then I realized, certain songs, the messages are eternal, nothing changes.
The climate has a lot to do with how you play. Maybe what you had for breakfast may affect how you play, maybe who you see, I don’t know. It’s a whole spiritual thing.

he_said_of_this_record.what_he_says: He said the trio record with his regular men, Alex Blake and Neil Clarke, is named for an ancient Egyptian phrase meaning 'the first time': the moment after silence when the creator gave us music, vibration by vibration. He repeated earlier songs such as 'Berkshire Blues'. It was recorded at a studio on the Lower East Side by an independent engineer, 'Rick Congress'.
he_said_of_this_record.title_meaning: Ancient Egyptian for 'the first time': when the creator first gave us music.
he_said_of_this_record.pull_quote: “Zep Tepi” is an ancient Egyptian word, it means “the first time”. It’s when the creator decided to give us music, because it was a time when there was just silence, there was nothing.

more_quotes.quote: All of the sudden there was one vibration, then two vibrations, then three vibrations, and these vibrations came to various kingdoms: the animal kingdom, the vegetable kingdom, and then man; man arrived.
That means when the creator gave us music for the first time, he gave us the foundation and from that up until 2009 the whole planet can share, express, and enjoy, what we call music.

he_said_of_this_record.discrepancies: 'Neil Clark' is Neil Clarke. 'Rick Congress' is unverified and may be misheard. The roles for Blake and Clarke are not stated in this block; I added them from the rest of the interview and identification.
